title: Spatiotemporal Patterns in Sex Ratios of Bat Fatalities at Wind Energy Facilities in the United States
abstract: A challenge facing bat conservation and wind energy development is how to maximize renewable energy production while minimizing impacts to bat populations. Reproductive-aged females are particularly important to dynamics and stability of bat populations due to their life history characteristics, but morphological sex identification methods have resulted in inaccurate reporting of sex ratios of fatalities at wind energy facilities. Our goal was to assess overall speciesspecific sex ratios of fatalities, and how those ratios varied by time and location. We used molecular techniques to determine the sex of 4445 carcasses of Brazilian free-tailed (Tadarida brasiliensis), evening (Nycticeius humeralis), hoary (Lasiurus cinereus), eastern red (Lasiurus borealis), northern yellow (Lasiurus intermedius), silver-haired (Lasionycteris noctivagans), and southern yellow (Lasiurus ega) bats found during turbine searches at 20 wind energy facilities in ten states in the United States between 2009 and 2022. Species composition and number of years of data varied by site. Overall, there were more fatalities of females than males for silver-haired and southern yellow bats, but not the other species. Brazilian free-tailed bat sex ratios were female skewed in late summer, whereas female skew occurred during portions of spring and summer/fall for eastern red bats, hoary, and silver-haired bats, and in spring and late fall for evening bats. In addition, spatial patterns in sex ratios existed for eastern red and hoary bats. The observed spatial and temporal patterns of fatalities can help target fatality reductions strategies to locations and times of year that maximize the conservation benefit of those actions.

## **1. Introduction**

A challenge facing bat conservation and wind energy development is how to maximize renewable energy production while

minimizing impacts to bat populations due to fatalities at wind turbines. Among bat species frequently reported as fatalities at wind energy facilities in the United States and Canada, hoary bats ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ), eastern red bats ( _Lasiurus borealis_ ), and silver-haired bats ( _Lasionycteris noctivagans_ ) have some of the highest estimated mortality rates (Arnett and Baerwald, 2013; Kunz et al., 2007; American Wind Wildlife Institute (AWWI), 2020). However, such estimates are based on an incomplete and geographically limited dataset, with few publicly available data from regions such as Texas, where a high proportion of North America’s wind turbines are located (Weaver et al., 2020b; Lloyd et al., 2023). Available data suggest that, for these species, wind turbine-related fatalities exceed other documented sources of direct anthropogenic fatality, such as intentional killing, accidents, and exposure to contaminants (O’Shea et al., 2016). These species are long-lived and have low annual reproductive rates (Barclay and Harder, 2003), and, as such, turbine collisions have potential to threaten their long-term persistence (Arnett et al., 2016; Frick et al., 2017; Friedenberg and Frick, 2021).

Although patterns related to the seasonal timing of fatalities and the extent to which different bat species are impacted has been well documented in the literature (e.g., Arnett and Baerwald, 2013; Arnett et al., 2016; Lloyd et al., 2023), evidence on sex differences or other vulnerabilities to collision fatality are limited. A recent study found that wind turbine fatality in Nathusius’ pipistrelles ( _Pipistrellus nathussi_ ) is biased toward females which may reflect a sex bias in the population due to migratory behavior of females in coastal areas where wind turbines are concentrated (Kruszynski et al., 2022). Increased female mortality is of conservation concern because females are particularly important to the stability and annual reproductive rates of bat populations for several reasons: (1) most bat species have a polygamous mating system; (2) female bats carry, nurse, and raise young; and (3) females of some species have multiple pups per litter (Ammerman et al., 2019). Therefore, activities that reduce the relative abundance of females are likely to cause more significant population declines (Grubler et al., 2008; Wedekind, 2012) than those that affect relatively more males. A more comprehensive understanding of sex differences and vulnerabilities to wind turbine fatality will likely improve our understanding of the population-level impacts and could help target minimization measures to where they could have the greatest impact on population stability. A once commonly held view was that males comprise _>_ 50 % of bat fatalities at wind energy facilities in North America (e.g., Arnett et al., 2008; Fiedler, 2004; Johnson et al., 2009). These studies relied on morphological sex identification of bat carcasses collected in the field – a method that produces inaccurate sex ratio estimates, especially for carcasses discovered more than one day after the fatality occurred (Korstian et al., 2013; Nelson et al., 2018; Chipps et al., 2020a). In fact, morphologically based misclassifications are not random. Instead, they significantly overestimate the relative abundance of males because relatively more females are misidentified or classified as being of unknown sex (Korstian et al., 2013; Chipps et al., 2020a). Given that most bat carcasses collected in the field are discovered more than one day after their arrival, genetic approaches are more reliable for accurate determination of sex of bat carcasses. Because of the nascent state of knowledge of this problem, many questions about the sex ratios of bat fatalities at wind energy facilities remain.

Our goal was to assess overall species-specific sex ratios of fatalities, including their seasonal and geographic patters. An improved understanding of these patterns is essential for informing appropriate and meaningful bat fatality minimization strategies. Sex-biased minimization strategies, such as implementing curtailment during periods of high risk to females, may be more cost-effective than curtailment based on uninformed sex ratio data while providing similar or even better population-level benefits. However, this may only be true if these periods of high female risk also coincide with overall periods of higher fatality risk, or if pregnant or nursing females are disproportionately killed which could affect recruitment and not accurately reflect the true number of fatalities due to death of pups. To address this topic, we used genetic markers to quantify sex ratios of carcasses of seven bat species obtained from wind energy facilities in the United States We specifically aimed to identify the temporal scale and geographic locations when the ratio of female to male fatalities was greatest, at the finest resolution possible given the uneven distribution of the available data (i.e., more carcasses were available for some locations compared to others, and for some weeks compared to others). Because bats have sexspecific behavioral strategies related to reproduction and roosting, we expected that sex ratios of bat carcasses found at wind energy facilities would vary by species, seasonal timing, and location. Support for this expectation would suggest that strategies to reduce fatalities of female bats may need to vary accordingly.

## **2. Methods**

## _2.1. Focal species & sample collection_

We focused on seven bat species known to commonly experience fatalities at wind turbines in the United States where they overlap with their range, including Brazilian free-tailed ( _Tadarida brasiliensis_ ), eastern red, evening ( _Nycticeius humeralis_ ), hoary, northern yellow ( _Lasiurus intermedius_ ), silver-haired, and southern yellow ( _L. ega_ ) bats. As previously mentioned, hoary, eastern red, and silverhaired bats comprise the majority of reported fatalities at utility-scale wind energy facilities (American Wind Wildlife Institute (AWWI) (AWWI), 2020; Lloyd et al., 2023), though it is important to again note that a reporting bias exists (Weaver et al., 2020b; Lloyd et al., 2023), and that species such as Brazilian free-tailed, evening, and northern yellow bats can suffer regionally high mortality rates (American Wind Wildlife Institute (AWWI) (AWWI), 2020; Weaver et al., 2020b; LiCari et al., 2023; Lloyd et al., 2023). Finally, as wind energy production expands in the southwestern U.S., tree-roosting species like the northern yellow and southern yellow bat and the migratory Brazilian free-tailed bat are expected to experience increased fatalities (Chipps et al., 2020b; Weaver et al., 2020b; Huang et al., 2024).

We included carcasses that were collected during post-construction bat fatality monitoring studies (PCM) conducted by the authors or PCM studies conducted by others with data provided to the authors by wind energy operators and consultants prior to, or as part of, a solicitation effort for this study. Carcasses and samples came from six wind energy facilities in Texas, three each in Illinois and Ohio,

two in Kansas, and one each in California, Indiana, Iowa, Maryland, West Virginia, and Wyoming (Table 1; Fig. 1 & 2). While these data provide valuable insights into bat fatalities at wind energy facilities, they are not derived from a random or comprehensive year-round sample of all wind energy facilities in the United States Thus, caution should be used in extrapolating broader population-level inferences from these findings. In most cases, species were identified morphologically in the field during PCM studies. Due to difficulties differentiating yellow bat species using morphology, all yellow bats were identified to species using genetic markers (Chipps et al., 2020a).

## _2.2. Laboratory analyses_

We extracted DNA with Qiagen DNeasy blood and tissue kits (Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA), or with methods reported in Korstian et al. (2013) and LiCari et al. (2023). We determined sex by amplifying the _zfx_ and _zfy_ introns found in the sex chromosomes using primers and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) parameters reported in Korstian et al. (2013). We visualized the amplified regions using gel electrophoresis and identified sex based on the number of bands present in the sample. Females produce a single band corresponding to the X-chromosome intron (245 base pairs [bp]). Males produce two bands, one corresponding to the X-chromosome intron (245 bp) and one corresponding to the Y-chromosome intron (80 bp). Bands larger than ~300 bp were disregarded when determining sex.

## _2.3. Data analysis_

Many of the carcasses we considered were not associated with search schedules or bias trial data and so we were unable to assess fatality rates. We determined timing of fatalities by the date a carcass was discovered, adjusted by the estimated time of death identified when carcasses were collected during search efforts in the field. If time of death was a range, we adjusted by the maximum – estimate. For example, if a carcass was estimated to be 2 3 days old, we estimated the date of fatality event by subtracting 3 days from the date on which the carcass was found. For those analyses focused on time of death, we removed any samples with no estimated time of death or an estimated time of death of _>_ 14 days prior to discovery from the analyses. We then binned all samples to the week of each year in which the fatalities were estimated to have occurred.

We conducted two sets of analyses: (1) tests for overall species-specific differences in sex ratios in fatalities, and (2) models assessing temporal and spatial variation in sex ratios, by species. To assess whether the proportion of female fatalities differed from males for each species, we used binomial tests comparing the observed proportion of females to a null expectation of 0.50. These tests included all samples of that species with successfully extracted and amplified DNA, regardless of time or location. For each species, we report the estimated proportion of females ( _P_ female), 95 % confidence intervals (CI), and p-values.

To evaluate temporal and spatial patterns in sex ratios, the response variable was binomial distributed and included weekly counts of females and males per site per year. These models included only samples with known time of death and geographic location to at least the state level. We excluded any location with fewer than 20 weeks of carcass observations.

We first conducted random effects model selection, holding fixed effects constant, to identify the optimal random effects structure. For each species, we compared generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) with site as a random effect to generalized additive models (GAMs) without random effects, in both cases using maximum likelihood (ML) and corrected Akaike Information Criterion (AICc; Burnham and Anderson, 2002). We fit models using the mgcv package (Wood et al., 2016) in R version 4.5.0 (R Core Team, 2025) and selected the model with the lowest AICc.

Next, we conducted fixed effects model selection using the best random effects structure. To evaluate seasonal variation in sex ratios, we included week of year as a cubic regression spline (Wood, 2017), which balances model flexibility with computational efficiency. Weeks with no bat carcass observations were excluded. For spatial effects, we included state as a fixed effect. For yellow and evening bats, which were restricted to Texas, we modeled county as a fixed effect. In cases where carcasses came from facilities spanning two counties, we grouped those counties.

Zuur Final models were refit using mgcv restricted maximum likelihood (REML) for more accurate variance component estimation ( et al., 2009). We report smooth term effective degrees of freedom (edf) and p-values. An edf of 1 indicates a linear relationship while values _>_ 1 indicate a non-linear relationship, supporting the use of GAMs. For selected models, GAM estimates (β) represent the log odds of female relative to male fatalities. To facilitate interpretation of the effect of week, we applied the inverse logit transformation to the estimated smooth term for week and the associated 95 % confidence intervals, producing a curve of predicted female proportions over the time (Wood, 2017). We used a significance level of α = 0.05 for all binomial and model-based tests.

## **3. Results**

## _3.1. Field and lab data collection_

Our full dataset included 6247 bats found at 20 wind energy facilities (hereafter sites) in 10 states, although species occurrence varied by location. While the data spanned the period from 2009 to 2022, 13 of the 20 sites had data for only one year, three sites for two years, two sites for three years, and one site each with five and six years of data. We included only 4445 bats (Table 1) in summary analyses and binomial tests because the remainder had inaccurate location data, lacked information on estimated time of death, or because DNA failed to amplify from the sample (Table 2), and only 4253 bats in models assessing temporal and spatial patterns due to low sample sizes for certain locations (Tables 1 and 3). ## _3.2. Sex ratios of bats fatalities found at wind energy facilities_

Binomial tests indicated the overall sex ratios for silver-haired and southern yellow bats were female-skewed (silver-haired bat: _p_ female = 0.579, 95 % _CI_ 0.540–0.617, _p <_ 0.001; southern yellow bat: _p_ female = 0.630, 95 % _CI_ 0.531–0.721, _p_ = 0.009). Overall sex ratios were not different from 50:50 for the other species ( _p >_ 0.05; Table 1). While proportions, 95 % _CI,_ and p-values changed in some cases, these results remained the same when we ran tests with the reduced data set included in GAMs. We did not include spatial models for evening or yellow bats because sample sizes were too small. For all species, the model with no random effects had the lowest Tables S2–S8 AICc and was carried forward in fixed effects model selection (Appendix A: ). Additionally, the best fixed effects models for northern and southern yellow bats were the null model, indicating that inclusion of spatiotemporal predictors did not improve model fit, while selected models for the remaining five species include week or week and state (Appendix A: Tables S2–S8).

## **4. Discussion**

Our results indicate that overall wind turbine fatalities were higher for female than male silver-haired and southern yellow bats, and that there were varying temporal and/or spatial patterns of higher proportion female fatalities for five of the seven bat species. These results imply that implementing fatality minimization strategies targeted at female bats would be feasible, but would vary by species, time of year, and location. We detected temporal skew in sex ratios of fatalities for five species. Some temporal patterns were consistent with our expectation of seasonal differences, including significantly greater female fatalities during spring for eastern red, evening, hoary, and silver-haired bats, and during summer and/or fall for these species as well as for Brazilian free-tailed bats.

Spring coincides with pregnancy for temperate female bats (Cockrum, 1955; Crichton and Krutzsch, 2000; Neuweiler, 2000). Thus, Piorkowski female fatalities during this critical time could have more significant population impacts by affecting recruitment rates. and O’Connell (2010) reported fatalities of pregnant female Brazilian free-tailed and hoary bats discovered during PCM at a wind energy facility in Oklahoma and suggested that this concern could extend to additional species. While it is well documented that the number of bat fatalities is lower in spring than in summer and fall, spring monitoring frequency is often reduced when compared to summer and fall which could result in unreliable estimates of spring mortality rate (Arnett et al., 2008; Lloyd et al., 2023). suggest comparable spring through fall monitoring studies may be important for our understanding of population-level impacts. More complete monitoring in the summer could also help to determine if increased vulnerability of juvenile bats is common among migratory species. For example, Kruszynski et a. (2022) showed higher fatality rates in juvenile Nathusius’ pipistrelles, especially in inland areas where the species is known to breed. A decrease in juvenile recruitment into the adult population could also contribute to population declines, and the extent of juvenile vulnerability to wind turbine fatality remains largely unknown for North American bat species.

More Brazilian free-tailed bat female fatalities were reported from mid-August to late September irrespective of locations included in the analysis. This result may be partially due to more searches conducted in this period relative to spring. However, approximately 95 % of samples originated from Texas and the remaining 5 % from California, thus the data were geographically limited with respect to this species range and overlap with wind energy facilities (Fig. 2; Huang et a. 2024). Therefore, we recommend exercising caution when considering if temporal patterns apply outside of Texas. Brazilian free-tailed bats form large maternity colonies in Texas from spring through summer with female skewed migrant populations (Glass, 1982; McCracken, 2003; Wiederholt et al., 2013). In contrast, this species is considered non-migratory with an even sex ratio in the California population (Krutzsch, 1955; Davis, et al., 1962). Thus, we expected to find support for female-biased fatalities in Texas but not California. However, other studies have found female-biased sex ratios in fatalities of this species at some wind energy facilities in the migratory range. For example, Piorkowski and O’Connell (2010) reported female-biased fatalities of Brazilian free-tailed bats in Oklahoma from May to July in 2004 and 2005. LiCari et al. (2023) found geographic differences in sex ratios at wind energy facilities in southern Texas that varied by year. These studies suggest that differences in sex ratios at individual facilities could be explained by proximity to cave roosts which would be female-biased and proximity to bridge roosts which tend to be male-biased (Piorkowski and O’Connell, 2010; LiCari et al., 2023). Finally, the selected model for this species explained relatively little variation, suggesting that unaccounted factors may better explain the observed patterns.

Model results for eastern red and hoary bats suggested geographic patterns with significantly lower or higher female fatalities in certain locations. However, for all three species, samples had restricted geographic representation in some states. Eastern red bats had a lower proportion of female fatalities in Illinois and higher proportion in Texas, but the ratio did not differ from 50:50 in Indiana. Hoary bats in Indiana had a higher proportion of female fatalities, but the ratio did not differ from 50:50 in Illinois or Texas. Samples for species found in Illinois and Indiana were restricted spatially (Fig. 1 & 2). As such, caution is advised when applying these results to other regions. Additional samples from PCM studies that have been or are being conducted would allow for stronger inference regarding both temporal and spatial trends.

Cryan (2003) assessed the seasonal distribution of eastern red, hoary, and silver-haired bats from museum records across North America and found eastern red bats did not segregate by sex. Therefore, our results in Illinois and Texas are somewhat unexpected. Additionally, Cryan (2003) reported hoary and silver-haired bats did show segregation of the sexes in the eastern portion of their ranges, which overlaps with the Midwestern states in our study, but noted some locations had even sex ratios for silver-haired bats and suggested certain populations might not migrate. This supports our findings of no spatial patterns for silver-haired bats. Furthermore, hoary bat males are thought to occur in more mountainous areas than females (Cryan, 2003), and Hayes et al. (2015) found growing season and temperatures might be important factors influencing differences in male and female seasonal distributions. Although assessing landscape level and climatic variables influencing sex ratios of bat fatalities was outside of our objectives, the higher proportion of female fatalities in Indiana for hoary bats, but no spatial patterns for silver-haired bats from the same location could be explained by such factors. As wind energy expands in these states, patterns of fatalities may change due to the limited spatial footprint of carcasses acquired for this study (Fig. 1 & 2). However, locations where proportion of female fatalities was significantly higher may be good candidates for testing female-targeted minimization efforts for eastern red and hoary bats.

Identifying geographic patterns of bat sex ratios at the state or county level can be of value because state and local jurisdictions have the authority to establish regulatory guidelines and ordinances for wind energy development which could guide implementation of female targeted minimization strategies. However, ecologically, it is likely that habitat and climate patterns are more important given that bats do not recognize political boundaries (Cryan, 2003; Hayes et al., 2015; Lloyd et al., 2023). Lloyd et al. (2023) assessed seasonal bat fatality patterns in the United States by Level II North American ecoregions (https://www.epa.gov/eco-research/ ecoregions-north-america) and found peak fatalities varied temporally by ecoregion and species. In their study, Indiana, Illinois, and Ohio were in the Central USA Plains ecoregion. Had we assessed patterns at the same spatial scale, our discovery of state-level patterns would have been masked, suggesting Level II ecoregions could be too coarse to elucidate some patterns.

We are uncertain why the proportion of female fatalities was significantly greater for southern yellow bats but not for northern yellow bats. These species are considered sister taxa (Baker et al., 1988; Bickham, 1987; Kurta and Lehr, 1995) and exhibit some behavioral similarities, such as roosting behavior (Jimenez, 2016). Moreover, the samples for both species were collected from the same wind energy facilities in Texas, where they are sympatric. However, little is known about their natural history (Ammerman et al., 2012). For southern yellow bats, one explanation could be that females are attracted to wind turbines (Roeleke et al., 2016). Geographic separation of sexes could be another explanation, with relatively more female southern yellow bats residing in Texas, as has been reported for other bat species (Cryan, 2003; Ford et al., 2002). Differences in migratory strategy could also be an explanation; some studies suggest both species are potentially non-migratory in this region (Baker et al., 1971; Weaver et al., 2020b), whereas others propose that northern yellow bats are migratory and southern yellow bats are sedentary (Rojas-Herrera et al., 2023). The same explanations may also apply to silver-haired bats, which similarly exhibited a higher overall proportion of female fatalities compared to male. For Nathusius’ pipistrelles, the higher proportion of female fatalities at wind turbines is attributed to a female-biased sex ratio in the coastal migratory corridors along the German North Sea coastline (Kruszynski et al., 2022). For the southern yellow and silver-haired bats, it is currently not known whether this pattern reflects a true difference in vulnerability or a difference in sex ratio in the populations.

Although we collected samples from ten states, sample sizes for certain species in specific locations were low, and there are numerous areas and time periods from which no samples were obtained. Part of this is due to exclusion of samples lacking time of death estimates, but we also had difficulties obtaining samples from some geographic regions. While eastern red, Brazilian free-tailed, and evening bats have somewhat restricted ranges in the United States (Arroyo-Cabrales et al., 2016; Barquez et al., 2015; Solari, 2019), they do overlap with many wind energy facilities in states from which we did not receive samples (Fig. 2; Hoen et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2024). Lack of samples from these locations could be due to few fatalities of each species occurring in each region (e.g., evening bats are not common fatalities in most Midwest facilities [American Wind Wildlife Institute (AWWI) (AWWI), 2020) and the lack of carcasses submitted to repositories. In most cases, carcasses are used for bias trials or disposed of at the end of the study per most state permit conditions. Future studies would benefit from collaboration among operators and agencies to establish repositories to save carcasses or if this is not feasible, collecting tissue and hair samples so that these valuable data can be used by the research community.

## **5. Conclusions**

This study determined the sex of several thousand bat carcasses found at wind energy facilities from 10 states in the United States. Depending on the population sizes and growth rates of silver-haired and southern yellow bats (which are currently unknown), the relatively high proportion of female fatalities for these species could be influencing population stability. Thus, minimization efforts to reduce fatalities of these species (particularly in the middle of spring and late summer for silver-haired bats) may benefit their populations. Furthermore, our results suggest that minimization activities could benefit female Brazilian free-tailed bat populations from mid-August to late September, eastern red bat populations from mid-April to early June and in August, evening bats from early to midApril and mid-September to mid-October, hoary bats in early to mid-May and August, and silver-haired bats in early to mid-May and mid- to late September. Additionally, for eastern red and hoary bats there was a significant decrease in the proportion of female fatalities from mid-September through mid- to late October which was the seasonal extent of our dataset.

Published standardized protocols for collecting and preserving carcasses and/or tissue samples from wildlife carcasses could be highly beneficial for use in research studies. These protocols would increase the availability of high quality, accurate data for answering priority research questions. We are aware of efforts to create collection nodes or repositories to facilitate submission of carcasses and/or tissue samples to designated storage facilities for further research such as this study, and to encourage establishment of such nodes. Our results indicate that adopting a weekly search frequency during spring monitoring would help reduce model

uncertainty. Additionally, future research on female reproductive status (e.g., pregnancy) would help to better understand the bio’s logical significance of spring female fatalities and to inform demographic modeling tools, such as the United States Geological Survey BatTool (Wiens et al., 2023). While BatTool is not currently capable of incorporating this information, it could be adjusted to do so in the future (A. Wiens, personal communication, March 10, 2025). We also suggest further research on demographics and life history to confirm the patterns we have discovered and to assess potential drivers. Despite concerted efforts from the authors and the Renewable Energy Wildlife Institute (REWI), we were unable to obtain spatially representative samples and many regions with wind energy facilities were not represented in this study. This highlights the importance of data and/or carcass sharing with museums and researchers, so these valuable data are not lost. Many remaining questions might already be answered, and solutions discovered regarding bat fatalities at wind turbines if researchers had more access to data from wind energy facilities. Finally, there are remaining research opportunities to determine if patterns discovered in this study apply to other wind resource regions.
